articles.title: New car sales in South Africa rose 15.7% in 2025 - TimesLIVE
articles.description: South Africa sold 597,338 new vehicles in 2025, up 15.7% year on year. India and China together supplied nearly 80% of the country's light vehicle imports.
articles.content:
South Africa sold 597,338 new vehicles in 2025, 15.7% more than a year earlier, when 516,103 vehicles were sold. In September 2025, monthly sales reached 54,700 vehicles, the highest figure in 10 years. A column for TimesLIVE notes that passenger car sales that month totalled 38,603 units, the highest since October 2014.
Imports from India and China
According to the Automotive Trade Manual of the Naamsa association, South Africa imported 391,287 light vehicles in 2025, 28.6% more than the 304,175 units imported the previous year. India was the largest supplier, delivering 219,796 vehicles, or 56.2% of all imports. China supplied another 91,326 vehicles, accounting for 23.3% of imported light vehicles.
Combined, India and China provided nearly 80% of South Africa's light vehicle imports. The number of Chinese brands on the country's new-car market rose from eight in 2024 to 15 in 2025. Last year, buyers could choose from 56 light vehicle brands and 1,995 model variants.
More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.
Competition and employment
Martle Keyter, CEO of operations at the Motor Industry Staff Association, named lower interest rates, improved access to credit, pent-up demand for vehicle replacements, and competition from affordable Chinese-brand vehicles and cars imported from India among the factors behind the market's revival.
In her assessment, sales growth creates work not only for dealers but also for service-centre employees, technicians, apprentices, advisers, financing and insurance specialists, parts sellers, and repair workshops. More than 311,000 workers are officially registered within the scope of the industry's collective bargaining council.
Keyter also believes that growing demand for new vehicles should be accompanied by investment in local production, supplier development, and skills transfer under South Africa's automotive plan through 2035.

articles.title: India orders coal plants to run at full capacity
articles.description: India orders coal plants to run at full capacity
articles.content:
NEW DELHI:
India has ordered more than 100 captive coal-fired power plants to operate at maximum capacity from October 1 through year-end to meet what it expects will be a rise in electricity demand.
The federal power ministry's order, invoked under emergency provisions of the Electricity Act, applies to plants with installed capacity of at least 50 megawatts. The aim is to meet an "expected rise in electricity demand in the coming months," showed the order dated September 25 and seen by Reuters. Nearly 40% of coal-fired plants are operating with critically low fuel stock due to a surge in power demand as the El Nino climate phenomenon raises temperatures more than usual.
The plants primarily serve industrial facilities such as aluminium smelters, steel manufacturers, cement factories and oil refineries. The power ministry has directed generators to sell surplus electricity through power exchanges.
The order covers 112 plants belonging to companies including Vedanta, Tata Steel, Hindalco Industries, JSW Steel, UltraTech Cement, Reliance Industries, Indian Oil, Bharat Aluminium, Hindustan Zinc and Nayara Energy.
The ministry has ordered plants to report weekly to the Central Electricity Authority detailing generation, captive consumption, power sales, available capacity and coal stocks.
Separately, the ministry has extended an earlier emergency order requiring Tata Power's imported coal-fired plant in Mundra, Gujarat to operate at full capacity until December 31, citing the demand situation.
Section 11 of the Electricity Act allows the government, under extraordinary circumstances, to direct generators to operate power stations in accordance with its instructions.

articles.title: DBS removes points transfers to Qantas Frequent Flyer
articles.description: DBS credit cards no longer offer points transfers to Qantas Frequent Flyer, leaving KrisFlyer and Asia Miles as the only realistic options.
articles.content:
Back in 2019, DBS added Qantas Frequent Flyer as its fourth transfer partner, allowing cardholders to convert points to a second oneworld partner after Cathay Pacific. Landing a partnership with Singapore’s largest bank was quite the coup for the Australian carrier, given that the only other transfer option at the time was with Citi.
Unfortunately, seven years later, that partnership has quietly come to an end.
DBS removes transfers to Qantas Frequent Flyer
Earlier this week, a MileLion community member spotted that Qantas Frequent Flyer had disappeared from the DBS rewards portal. I checked with DBS whether this was just a temporary glitch or a permanent removal, and a spokesperson confirmed it was the latter.
This leaves DBS cardholders with just three transfer options — though it’s really more like two, since AirAsia Rewards won’t be of much interest to most miles collectors.
Frequent Flyer Programme Conversion Ratio
(DBS Points : Miles) 5,000:10,000 5,000:10,000 500:1,500
I doubt there’ll be many tears shed over the removal, given that the vast majority of DBS Points redemptions are no doubt for KrisFlyer and Asia Miles. In fact, the likely reason Qantas was dropped was because the low take-up rate didn’t justify the costs of maintaining the partnership.
That said, I did make use of this option a couple of years back by redeeming Qantas Points for a domestic flight on WestJet. At just 10,000 points per passenger, it was pretty good value, given that cash fares were almost S$300 and I needed the flexibility of being able to cancel.
How else can you earn Qantas Points?
If you want to continue earning Qantas Points, the following programmes still offer transfers.
Programme Conversion Ratio
(Programme Points : Qantas) 500:250 (Plat Charge, Centurion)
550:250 (All others)
⚡ Instant 10,000:10,000 (Citi Miles)
25,000:10,000 (Citi ThankYou Points) 25,000:10,000
⚡ Instant
What are Qantas Points good for?
I don’t consider myself an expert on Qantas Frequent Flyer, but some of the better uses of Qantas Points are for:
Short-haul Economy Class flights on Qantas and American Airlines (<600 miles): 9,200 points
Short-haul Jetstar flights (<600 miles): 5,700 points
Oneworld round-the-world bookings (of up to 35,000 miles): 152,200 points in Economy, 365,800 points in Business
Qantas Frequent Flyer members also get the best access to Qantas First Class award availability, with bookings opening 353 days in advance (compared to other partners like American Airlines, which opens 331 days in advance).
Full list of transfer partners
Here’s the updated list of transfer partners for each bank in Singapore, following the removal of Qantas Frequent Flyer.
To learn more about the various options, refer to the post below.
Complete list of Singapore credit card airline and hotel transfer partners
Conclusion
DBS has removed Qantas Frequent Flyer as a transfer partner, which effectively reduces cardholders to just KrisFlyer and Asia Miles — though those are probably the two most important options to have anyway.
Given the limited appeal of the programme to a Singapore resident, it doesn’t really change how I rate DBS cards. If you really need Qantas Points, American Express, Citi and HSBC still offer avenues for conversions.
